title: the summit sit
hook: a shelf holds a string of beads, a candle stub, a folded blanket and a card of Sanskrit letters

segments.voice: Yesterday the summit sit went back to the three tracks, and the lotus leaf that sits in the water and stays dry. Did you lift your hands off one finished task? Today, the practices. Day one thousand fifty-two.

A string of beads, worn smooth in one spot. A candle burned down to a stub. A blanket, folded, that someone lay under with their eyes closed. A card with Sanskrit letters on it, the vowels first. Put them on one shelf and you have the last block of practice from this year: breath, mantra, rest, gaze, hands and sound. Today's summit sit climbs back to that shelf, and instead of talking about the practices, it does a little of each.
screen: `BEADS, A CANDLE, A BLANKET, A CARD.` → `ONE SHELF.` → `THE PRACTICES, DEEPER.`

segments.voice: First, the shelf by name. Pranayama sequences: shaping the breath. Mantra sadhana: a sacred sound repeated on the beads, day after day. Yoga nidra: lying still and letting the body be scanned and released while awareness stays awake. Trataka: a still gaze on one small point. The mudras: the hands held in a shape that means something. And Sanskrit sounds: the alphabet heard before it is read. Six practices. Looked at from the top, they share one direction. Each takes something that usually runs on its own, the breath, the tongue, the body, the eyes, the hands, the voice, and asks it to do one thing on purpose for a while. The Yoga Sutra has a short line about what makes any practice hold. In paraphrase: practice becomes firmly grounded when it's kept up for a long time, without breaks, and with care. Long, unbroken, and with care. Notice what that line doesn't ask for. It doesn't ask for hard, or impressive, or perfect. The word for this kind of steady practice, the word that sits behind this whole block, is sadhana. A sadhana is the practice you return to, the one that becomes yours by being done. The beads get smooth in one spot because the same fingers keep coming back. So today the summit sit isn't a review in words. It's a short sadhana that borrows one breath from each part of the shelf.
screen: `SIX PRACTICES ON ONE SHELF.` · `EACH ASKS ONE THING, ON PURPOSE.` · `LONG, UNBROKEN, WITH CARE.` · `SADHANA: THE PRACTICE YOU RETURN TO.` · then, large: `A LITTLE OF EACH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Let one breath out run a little longer than the breath in. Rest the thumb and first finger of each hand together, the others relaxed. Let your eyes find one small point in front of you and stay there gently, blinking when you need to. Then let them close. If you keep a mantra, let it move quietly with the breath. If not, the open sound, ah, said silently. Feel the body grow heavy where it touches the floor or chair, and keep the watcher awake. Stay with all of it, lightly. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the practices, gathered into a single sit, a little of each.
Your line: the summit sit. Today, pick the one practice from that shelf you'd most like to keep, and give it one minute before bed. Day one thousand fifty-two.

howItsDone: Practitioners often keep a daily sadhana, a regular personal practice that may combine breathwork, japa on a mala, a gaze or a mudra, and quiet sitting, ideally at the same time each day.

myth: the Yoga Sutra says practice holds when it's hard and perfect
it says long, unbroken, and with care, not hard or perfect.
sadhana means the practice you keep returning to
it's the steady practice that becomes yours by being done.
yoga nidra means falling asleep on purpose
the body rests and is released while awareness stays awake.

fork.setup: you've tried six practices this year and want one to last. what does the Yoga Sutra's line point to?
options: the hardest one, done once a month.
whichever one, kept up long, without breaks, with care.
all six at once, for an hour a day.
fork.reveal: the sutra names three conditions: a long time, no breaks, and care. it says nothing about difficulty.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sadhana, a steady spiritual practice, the one you return to.

trapdoor: what you thought: deeper practice means harder practice.
what it means: a sadhana deepens by being kept up long, without breaks, and with care.
what a scholar hears: Yoga Sutra 1.14, dirgha-kala, nairantarya, satkara: long time, without interruption, with devotion.

notes: Sixth summit sit (1047–1053): revisits the practices-deeper block (1007–1046): pranayama sequences, mantra sadhana, yoga nidra, trataka, the mudras, Sanskrit sounds for readers. The 'six practices' count is of this curriculum's own block, not a claim about a text.
Paraphrase of Yoga Sutra 1.14 (sa tu dirgha-kala-nairantarya-satkara-asevito dridha-bhumih). Confirm 'with care' for satkara (often 'with devotion' or 'earnestness').

The combined practice uses chin or jnana mudra (thumb and index finger together) without naming it, and a silent 'ah' for those without a mantra (linked to day 1040's 'a'); the longer out-breath is a gentle general instruction. Confirm safety and fit.
Gloss of sadhana as 'the practice you return to' is descriptive, not an etymology; check.
